summary: Go SDK streaming tool-callback: webhook HMAC signature mismatch after proxy timestamp truncation causing duplicate tool executions on retry
description:
Issue summary:
NimbleDocs is seeing duplicated downstream tool executions (webhook target receives same tool invocation twice) when a streaming generation triggers a function/tool call. The Go SDK client receives a transient signature verification error from the webhook endpoint on the first delivery, performs a retry, and the webhook ends up executing the side effect twice.

Impact:
- Intermittent duplicate processing of invoices in customer's system (customer reports ~2-3% of requests duplicating over the past 48h).
- Affects production traffic on their Dedicated cluster in us-west-2.

Environment:
- Customer using Redwood Go SDK v0.8.3 with streaming and func_call support enabled.
- Dedicated deployment (customer-owned VPC) with API Gateway + edge proxy (third-party WAF) in front of customer webhook.

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Start a stream with a tool call that posts to https://hooks.nimbledocs.com/rdw-callback
2) We observe the SDK sending callback with headers: X-Redwood-TS, X-Redwood-Signature (HMAC-SHA256).
3) The customer's WAF strips millisecond precision from the timestamp header (X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234 -> 1678901234).
4) Customer server calculates HMAC using original timestamp (with ms) and signature validation fails.
5) Server returns 401 -> Redwood SDK performs immediate retry for callback delivery -> server accepts second delivery and executes tool action.

Expected behavior:
- SDK retries should not cause duplicate side effects for non-idempotent endpoints if the first delivery might have actually been processed (or should include guidance to make webhooks idempotent).

Actual behavior:
- Some webhook endpoints reject the first callback because of timestamp rounding/truncation by intermediaries, causing client retries that lead to duplicate downstream side effects.

Relevant logs (sanitized):
- SDK outbound attempt 1 headers:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234.789
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=ab12...
- Edge/WAF observed header rewrite:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234
- Customer server log: "signature mismatch: calculated=cd34... received=ab12..." -> returns 401.
- SDK outbound attempt 2 (retry) headers:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901235.102
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=ef56...
- Customer server accepts and processes the callback on attempt 2.

Attachments: customer provided packet capture showing header truncation and sample SDK trace token.
comments: 2026-03-12 10:22 - Support (Aisha): Opened with initial triage and requested packet captures and example webhook logs from customer.
2026-03-12 14:05 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Uploaded packet capture showing WAF middleware truncating X-Redwood-TS. Confirmed duplicates occur ~2% of calls.

2026-03-13 09:10 - Eng (Marcus): Reproduced locally by inserting a proxy that truncates timestamp header; observed identical signature verification failure followed by retry leading to duplicate POSTs to origin.

2026-03-13 11:40 - SRE (Lin): Noted that SDK currently includes full-ms timestamp and server-side validation expects exact match — there's no replay cache for callbacks at customer endpoint by default.
2026-03-14 08:12 - Support (Aisha): Proposed mitigations to customer and engineering follow-ups (see investigation notes and resolution).
investigation_notes: Reproduction steps performed in internal staging: Go SDK v0.8.3 streaming client -> local proxy that truncates X-Redwood-TS to seconds -> origin validates signature with ms precision -> origin returns 401 -> SDK retries with new timestamp -> origin accepts second call. Result: duplicate execution observed.

Root cause: mismatch between the timestamp canonicalization expected by customer's HMAC verification and header mutation by an intermediary. The SDK sends a fresh signature tied to the precise timestamp; if intermediary mutates timestamp before the origin, origin will reject first attempt even though SDK signed original value. SDK then retries and issues a second signed attempt which origin accepts. No deduplication layer on customer's webhook means side effect occurs twice.

Edge case: clock skew on origin could cause legitimate rejections; however packet capture shows clock aligned — truncation is the trigger. WAF (third-party) is rewriting headers for normalization/compatibility and dropping fractional seconds.

Potential SDK behavior change: include an idempotency token in callback body/headers separate from HMAC that downstream can use for deduplication; maintain short-lived replay cache on our callback delivery subsystem (danger: extra state and memory on Redwood side).

Customer constraints: they cannot add a replay cache on origin side easily because their processing pipeline is third-party-managed. They prefer guidance to harden webhook validation logic to tolerate timestamp normalization.
Related internal links: linked SUP-473901 (retry-scope-enforcement-mismatch) may have useful context on header normalization patterns.
resolution:
Workaround provided to customer (2026-03-14):
1) Update webhook signature validation to allow for a configurable timestamp tolerance and to validate HMAC against both raw and truncated timestamp variants when the request originates from known proxies. Example pseudo-logic: accept if HMAC matches signature(timestamp_ms) OR signature(timestamp_seconds).
2) Implement idempotency check on webhook consumer using X-Redwood-Callback-Id header (we recommended customer check this header when deciding whether to execute side effects).
3) As short-term, whitelist Redwood delivery IPs on their WAF or configure the WAF to preserve X-Redwood-TS header without truncation.

Engineering follow-up (internal):
- Action item ENG-11273: Evaluate adding an X-Redwood-Callback-Id header to all SDK callback deliveries (low-risk), targeted for SDK v0.9.x.
- Action item ENG-11274: Investigate a transient dedupe cache in the callback delivery path; document operational cost/limits.
- Action item DOCS-5568: Add guidance to webhook best practices for handling timestamp normalization and idempotency patterns (include signature verification tolerant patterns and sample code for Go/Python/TS).
Status: Workaround accepted by customer. Engineering tickets created and tagged for Q2 prioritization. Keeping this support ticket open while ENG checks feasibility and until docs are published.
Final customer note: NimbleDocs implemented header-tolerance logic and reported a drop to ~0.05% duplicates over 24h after change (2026-03-14 18:30).
